theory.intro: **Dependent events** are events where earlier outcomes change later probabilities. For random draws from the same finite collection **without replacement**, the first item is not put back, so the second draw has one fewer item to choose from. Build the tree as before, but rewrite the second-stage fractions.
facts: **Dependent events** occur when an earlier result changes the probabilities at a later stage. Random draws from the same finite collection without replacement are an example.
For random draws from the same finite collection without replacement, at the second draw the total has fallen by $1$, so every second-stage denominator is one less than the first-stage denominator.
From $3$ red and $5$ blue, drawing red first leaves $\frac{2}{7}$ red and $\frac{5}{7}$ blue on the second-stage branches.
The branches leaving any one point still add to $1$: $\frac{2}{7} + \frac{5}{7} = 1$.
Multiply along a path and add the paths that satisfy the event, exactly as for independent stages.
Unless the question asks for another form, give the probability as a fraction in simplest form.
steps: Draw a tree with one set of branches for each draw.
Label the first-stage branches from the original totals.
Label the second-stage branches after removing the item already drawn.
Multiply along the branches of each path.
Add the paths that satisfy the event.

workedExamples.question_text: A bag contains $6$ red and $3$ blue counters. Two counters are drawn at random without replacement. Complete a probability tree for the two draws. Explain how the second-stage probabilities change after a red counter is drawn.

A box contains $4$ lemon and $7$ strawberry lollies. Two lollies are chosen at random without replacement. Find the probability of:
a. two lemon lollies
b. a lemon lolly followed by a strawberry lolly.
workedExamples.solution_text:
a. After choosing a lemon lolly, $3$ lemon lollies remain among $10$ lollies.

$\begin{align*}P(LL)&=\frac{4}{11}\times\frac{3}{10}\\&=\frac{12}{110}\\&=\frac{6}{55}\end{align*}$

b. Choosing a lemon lolly leaves all $7$ strawberry lollies among the $10$ remaining lollies.

$\begin{align*}P(LS)&=\frac{4}{11}\times\frac{7}{10}\\&=\frac{28}{110}\\&=\frac{14}{55}\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: A bag contains $4$ green and $5$ pink counters. Two counters are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability of drawing one counter of each colour, in any order.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The two possible colour orders are green then pink and pink then green. Multiply along each path.

$\begin{align*}P(GP)&=\frac{4}{9}\times\frac{5}{8}\\&=\frac{20}{72}\end{align*}$

$\begin{align*}P(PG)&=\frac{5}{9}\times\frac{4}{8}\\&=\frac{20}{72}\end{align*}$

Add the two path probabilities.

$\begin{align*}P(\text{one of each})&=\frac{20}{72}+\frac{20}{72}\\&=\frac{40}{72}\\&=\frac{5}{9}\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: A bag contains $5$ red, $4$ blue and $3$ green counters. Two counters are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability that both counters are the same colour.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The matching-colour paths are $RR$, $BB$ and $GG$.

$\begin{align*}P(RR)&=\frac{5}{12}\times\frac{4}{11}\\&=\frac{20}{132}\end{align*}$

$\begin{align*}P(BB)&=\frac{4}{12}\times\frac{3}{11}\\&=\frac{12}{132}\end{align*}$

$\begin{align*}P(GG)&=\frac{3}{12}\times\frac{2}{11}\\&=\frac{6}{132}\end{align*}$

Add all three path probabilities.

$\begin{align*}P(\text{same colour})&=\frac{20}{132}+\frac{12}{132}+\frac{6}{132}\\&=\frac{38}{132}\\&=\frac{19}{66}\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text:
A shelf holds $7$ novels and $5$ science books. Two books are selected at random. Find the probability of selecting two novels:
a. when the first book is replaced before the second selection
b. when the first book is not replaced.
workedExamples.solution_text:
a. With replacement, there are again $7$ novels among $12$ books for the second selection.

$\begin{align*}P(\text{two novels})&=\frac{7}{12}\times\frac{7}{12}\\&=\frac{49}{144}\end{align*}$

b. Without replacement, selecting a novel leaves $6$ novels among $11$ books.

$\begin{align*}P(\text{two novels})&=\frac{7}{12}\times\frac{6}{11}\\&=\frac{42}{132}\\&=\frac{7}{22}\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: A bag contains $5$ yellow and $4$ white counters. Three counters are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability that all three counters are the same colour.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The required paths are $YYY$ and $WWW$. Each draw removes one counter, so the totals are $9$, $8$ and $7$.

$\begin{align*}P(YYY)&=\frac{5}{9}\times\frac{4}{8}\times\frac{3}{7}\\&=\frac{60}{504}\end{align*}$

$\begin{align*}P(WWW)&=\frac{4}{9}\times\frac{3}{8}\times\frac{2}{7}\\&=\frac{24}{504}\end{align*}$

Add the two path probabilities.

$\begin{align*}P(\text{same colour})&=\frac{60}{504}+\frac{24}{504}\\&=\frac{84}{504}\\&=\frac{1}{6}\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: A bag contains $4$ grey, $3$ yellow and $5$ white counters. Three counters are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability of drawing two grey counters and one white counter, in any order.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Let $G$ mean grey and $W$ mean white. The required orders are $GGW$, $GWG$ and $WGG$.

$\begin{align*}P(GGW)&=\frac{4}{12}\times\frac{3}{11}\times\frac{5}{10}\\&=\frac{60}{1320}\end{align*}$

$\begin{align*}P(GWG)&=\frac{4}{12}\times\frac{5}{11}\times\frac{3}{10}\\&=\frac{60}{1320}\end{align*}$

$\begin{align*}P(WGG)&=\frac{5}{12}\times\frac{4}{11}\times\frac{3}{10}\\&=\frac{60}{1320}\end{align*}$

Add all three path probabilities.

$\begin{align*}P(\text{two greys and one white})&=\frac{60}{1320}+\frac{60}{1320}+\frac{60}{1320}\\&=\frac{180}{1320}\\&=\frac{3}{22}\end{align*}$

foundation.question_text:
A bag contains $5$ red and $2$ blue counters.
Two counters are picked at random, one after the other without replacement.
Find the probability that both counters are red, as a fraction in simplest form.

A bag contains $3$ red and $5$ blue marbles.
Two marbles are taken out without replacement.
Find the probability that both marbles are blue, as a fraction in simplest form, then state what the second-stage blue branch would have been if the first marble had been replaced.
foundation.solution_text:
$P(BB) = \frac{5}{8} \times \frac{4}{7}$
$= \frac{20}{56}$
$= \frac{5}{14}$
With replacement the bag would again hold $5$ blue marbles out of $8$, so the second-stage blue branch would be $\frac{5}{8}$.

foundation.question_text:
A class has $12$ boys and $13$ girls.
Two students are chosen one after the other, and the same student cannot be chosen twice.
The first student chosen is a boy.
Write the probability that the second student chosen is a girl, as a fraction in simplest form.
foundation.solution_text:
One boy has already been chosen, so $13$ girls remain out of $24$ students.
$P(\text{second is a girl}) = \frac{13}{24}$

development.question_text:
A bookshelf holds $12$ novels and $9$ science books.
Two books are selected at random.
Find, as fractions in simplest form:
a. the probability of choosing two novels when the first book **is** replaced before the second is selected
b. the probability of choosing two novels when the first book is **not** replaced.
development.solution_text:
a. With replacement the shelf again holds $12$ novels out of $21$ books.
$P(\text{two novels}) = \frac{12}{21} \times \frac{12}{21}$
$= \frac{144}{441}$
$= \frac{16}{49}$
b. Without replacement only $11$ novels remain out of $20$ books.
$P(\text{two novels}) = \frac{12}{21} \times \frac{11}{20}$
$= \frac{132}{420}$
$= \frac{11}{35}$

development.question_text:
A bag contains $3$ grey, $2$ yellow and $5$ white counters.
One counter is taken out and it is yellow.
It is not replaced, and a second counter is taken out.
Write the probability that the second counter is white, as a fraction in simplest form.
development.solution_text:
A yellow counter has been removed, so the white count is unchanged: $5$ white counters remain out of $9$ counters.
$P(\text{second is white}) = \frac{5}{9}$

mastery.question_text:
A bag contains $3$ grey, $2$ yellow and $5$ white counters.
Three counters are taken out one after the other without replacement.
Find the probability of taking two grey counters and one white counter, as a fraction in simplest form.
mastery.solution_text:
4. **Multiply along the branches of each path**
$P(\text{grey, grey, white}) = \frac{3}{10} \times \frac{2}{9} \times \frac{5}{8}$
$= \frac{30}{720}$
The white counter could be taken first, second or third, so three paths each have probability $\frac{30}{720}$.
5. **Add the paths that satisfy the event**
$P(\text{two greys and a white}) = 3 \times \frac{30}{720}$
$= \frac{90}{720}$
$= \frac{1}{8}$

mastery.question_text:
A bag contains $4$ red, $3$ blue and $3$ green counters.
Two counters are taken out without replacement.
Find the probability that the two counters are the same colour, as a fraction in simplest form.
mastery.solution_text:
4. **Multiply along the branches of each path**
$P(RR) = \frac{4}{10} \times \frac{3}{9}$
$= \frac{12}{90}$
$P(BB) = \frac{3}{10} \times \frac{2}{9}$
$= \frac{6}{90}$
$P(GG) = \frac{3}{10} \times \frac{2}{9}$
$= \frac{6}{90}$
5. **Add the paths that satisfy the event**
$P(\text{same colour}) = \frac{12}{90} + \frac{6}{90} + \frac{6}{90}$
$= \frac{24}{90}$
$= \frac{4}{15}$
